commitResults.messageTitle: Add support for storing and listing tasks
Add support for todo, deadline, and event tasks
Handle empty todo description and unknown commands
Use a CommandType enum for command dispatch (A-Enums)
Save tasks to disk when list changes
Load tasks from disk on startup

commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline stores its "by" field as a plain String and prints
or saves it back exactly as the user typed it.

An arbitrary string like "June 6th" or "asap" is accepted
just as readily as a real date, so the chatbot can't
validate, compare, or reformat deadlines in any meaningful
way.

Let's parse the /by argument into a java.time.LocalDate at
input time, keep that as the stored representation, and
format it separately for display and for the save file.

LocalDate gives parsing and validation for free, rejects a
malformed date before it's ever stored, and gives later
features (like filtering tasks by date) something concrete
to compare against.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add on command to find tasks by date
commitResults.messageBody:
There's no way to see which tasks fall on a specific date;
the only option is to list everything and read through it
by hand.

As the list grows this gets tedious, and the LocalDate field
added to Deadline is otherwise write-only from the user's
point of view.

Let's add an "on DATE" command that filters tasks down to
whichever ones report a match via a new isOccurringOn()
method, defined on Task (default false) and overridden in
Deadline.

Checking task.isOccurringOn(date) keeps the filtering logic
on Task/Deadline rather than scattering instanceof checks
through Elora, and leaves room to extend the same capability
to Event later without touching the command-handling code.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui, Storage, Parser, TaskList classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Elora.java is one class holding roughly 330 lines: command
dispatch, every System.out.println call, and raw file
reading/writing, all mixed together in a single loop.

This makes each concern hard to test or reuse in isolation,
and any change - a wording tweak, a save-format tweak, a new
command - forces touching the same large method regardless of
which concern it actually belongs to.

Let's extract Ui (all reading and printing), Storage (loading
and saving the data file), Parser (turning raw input into a
command word, arguments, and a CommandType), and TaskList (the
task collection and its operations), leaving Elora to hold one
of each and orchestrate them in run().

Each class now has exactly one reason to change, and the
split follows the seams already visible in the old code -
println calls, file I/O calls, string-parsing calls, and
list-manipulation calls were each already grouped together,
just not separated into their own files.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into elora and elora.task packages
commitResults.messageBody:
All eleven classes sit in the default (unnamed) package,
directly under src/main/java, with no package declarations.

The Java coding standard requires every class to belong to a
named package, and grouping unrelated classes in the default
package doesn't scale as the codebase grows.

Let's split the classes into two packages: elora for the app
machinery (Elora, Ui, Storage, Parser, CommandType,
EloraException) and elora.task for the task domain model
(Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskList), moving each file with
git mv and adding the matching package declaration plus any
cross-package imports needed.

This groups task-related classes together, separate from what
drives the app itself, satisfies both the Minimal and Stretch
goal bars in one pass, and follows the same seam the A-MoreOOP
refactor already established.

build.gradle's application block still points mainClass at
seedu.duke.Duke, left over from the add-gradle-support branch
being created before the chatbot was renamed and repackaged.

With that stale value, ./gradlew run can't find the class and
fails to launch the application.

Let's update mainClass to elora.Elora, matching where the
entry point actually lives now.

This is the only change needed for Gradle's run task to work
- everything else in build.gradle (Java version, dependencies,
standard-input wiring) is already correct for this project.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Parser, Task, TaskList, Deadline
commitResults.messageBody:
The codebase has no automated tests; every method has only
been checked by hand-running the chatbot and reading its
console output.

Manual checking doesn't scale, and it's easy to silently
break an already-working method - a date-parsing edge case, an
off-by-one in TaskList - while changing something nearby
without ever noticing.

Let's add JUnit 5 tests for the classes with pure, side-effect-
free logic - Parser, Task, TaskList, and Deadline - covering
the command-parsing branches, done/not-done state transitions,
list add/remove/date-filtering, and Deadline's date formatting
and comparison.

These four classes hold most of the project's actual decision-
making logic and have no file or console I/O to work around,
making them the highest-value targets for JUnit. Ui, Storage,
and Elora are left for a later pass, since testing them
meaningfully needs mocked I/O or a temp filesystem rather than
straightforward method calls.

build.gradle's shadowJar task still names its output
duke.jar, left over from the add-gradle-support branch, from
before the chatbot was renamed.

Distributing a JAR called duke.jar for a chatbot named Elora
is confusing for anyone who downloads it from a release.

Let's rename shadowJar's archiveFileName to elora.jar,
matching the application's actual name.

This is a cosmetic rename only - the shadowJar task, mainClass,
and everything else needed to produce a working fat JAR were
already configured correctly during A-Gradle.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Javadoc to elora package classes
commitResults.messageBody:
None of the classes in the elora package have header comments;
a reader has to open each method body to learn what it does.

The coding standard requires header comments on public classes
and methods, and undocumented public methods force every caller
to read the implementation just to know what a method expects
or returns.

Let's add Javadoc to every class and public method in the elora
package (Elora, Ui, Storage, Parser, CommandType,
EloraException), following the format the standard specifies:
a summary sentence, a blank line, then @param/@return where
they add real value.

Simple getters and straightforward @Override methods are left
undocumented, consistent with the standard's own exemptions for
those two cases.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Javadoc to elora.task package classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, and TaskList have no header
comments either.

Same reason as the elora package: undocumented public methods
force readers into the implementation, and the coding standard
requires these comments.

Let's add the same treatment to the task-domain classes,
including describing each subclass's specific
toString()/toSaveFormat() format, since those differ
meaningfully from Task's base version rather than being an
exact override.

Kept as its own commit, separate from the elora package
changes, so each commit stays focused on one package - matching
the file organization A-Packages already established.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
There's no way to search the task list; finding a specific
task means reading through the whole list command output by
eye.

As the list grows this doesn't scale, and the assignment
specifically asks for keyword search.

Let's add a find command that filters tasks by a
case-insensitive substring match on their description,
following the same list-then-display pattern already used for
list and on.

Case-insensitive matching is more forgiving for the user than
requiring exact case, and this reuses the existing
TaskList/Ui separation rather than adding search logic
directly in Elora.

commitResults.messageTitle: Validate find keyword and handle no matches
commitResults.messageBody:
find with no keyword currently searches for an empty string,
silently matching every task; a search with zero results shows
a bare header with nothing under it.

Matching everything on an empty keyword is confusing since the
user's intent isn't clear, and a blank result under the header
for a genuine no-match case could look like a bug rather than a
deliberate outcome.

Let's reject an empty keyword the same way other commands
reject missing arguments, and print an explicit message when
nothing matches.

Keeps error handling consistent with how every other command
already validates its own arguments.

commitResults.messageTitle: Resolve leftover conflict markers in Storage.java
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage.java still contained unresolved <<<<<<< / ======= /
>>>>>>> conflict markers from an earlier merge, committed as
literal text instead of being resolved.

Literal conflict markers aren't valid Java, so the project
fails to compile.

Let's replace the file with its correct, fully-merged content -
the Javadoc from A-JavaDoc plus the line-wrap from
A-CodingStandard, with nothing left over from either side's
markers.

Verified by recompiling the whole project and re-running the
full regression test after this fix.

CommandType had FIND defined, but Parser, TaskList, Ui, and
Elora were missing the rest of the find command's
implementation - the command-word mapping, the search logic,
the display method, and the switch case that wires them
together.

As a result, typing find returned "I don't recognize that one
yet" instead of searching, even though part of the merge had
apparently gone through.

Let's bring all four files to their complete, correct state:
Javadoc throughout, the line-wraps from A-CodingStandard, and
the full find implementation from Level-9.

Verified by compiling clean and running find book directly,
which now returns the matching task as expected.

commitResults.messageTitle: Wire up Checkstyle with the seedu Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project already follows the seedu-java-coding-standard by hand,
but nothing enforces it automatically - a violation can slip in and
sit unnoticed until a manual review catches it.

Add Gradle's checkstyle plugin, pointed at the same config used by
AddressBook Level 3 (config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml, copied
verbatim from se-edu/addressbook-level3), which encodes that same
standard: import order, naming conventions, brace placement,
Javadoc presence, 120-char line length, indentation, and so on.
suppressions.xml (also from AB3) exempts test classes from the
Javadoc-presence checks, since test methods are self-documenting by
name.

`./gradlew check` (and therefore `build`) now runs checkstyleMain
and checkstyleTest alongside the JUnit tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix Checkstyle indentation violations in switch statements
commitResults.messageBody:
Running checkstyleMain surfaced 198 IndentationCheck violations, all
in the three classes with switch statements (Elora, Parser,
Storage). The config's caseIndent="4" expects each case label
indented one level deeper than its switch, with the case body
indented one level deeper still; these switches instead kept case
labels flush with switch, Eclipse-formatter style.

Reindented the body of each switch by one level to match. No
behavioural change - confirmed by `./gradlew build` still passing
all 27 tests with zero Checkstyle violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor command execution to return responses instead of printing
commitResults.messageBody:
A GUI can't reuse a command loop that talks directly to
System.out/System.in - it needs the response as a String it can put
in a chat bubble. Ui's show* methods printed directly, and the
switch in Elora.run() was entangled with the console loop (reading
input, printing dividers, tracking isExit).

Change every Ui show* method into a *Message method that returns the
formatted String instead of printing it. Extract the switch itself
out of run() into a private executeCommand(String), which parses one
line of input and returns Elora's reply (or throws EloraException on
bad input) with no console I/O of its own.

run() now just prints whatever executeCommand returns and stops on
"bye" - preparing the ground for a getResponse(String) entry point
that a GUI can call directly. No behavioural change for the existing
CLI; all 27 tests still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX GUI for Elora
commitResults.messageBody:
Give Elora a chat-style window instead of requiring the console,
built on the JavaFX runtime bundled in the Azul FX JDK distribution
(25.0.3.fx-zulu) - no org.openjfx.javafxplugin needed since the
javafx.* modules are already on this JDK's module path.

- Main (extends Application) loads MainWindow.fxml and wires it to
  an Elora instance via getResponse()/getWelcomeMessage(), added in
  the previous commit's refactor.
- Launcher is a plain-class entry point separate from Main, so
  running the shadowJar doesn't hit the "JavaFX runtime components
  are missing" failure some setups get when the jar's Main-Class
  itself extends Application.
- MainWindow is the FXML controller: it appends a DialogBox for each
  user message and Elora's reply, auto-scrolls to the bottom, and
  exits via Platform.exit() once elora.isExitCommand() sees "bye".
- DialogBox is a custom HBox control (loaded via fx:root, required
  when combining setRoot()+setController() on a control that isn't
  a plain FXML document) showing an avatar next to a speech bubble;
  getEloraDialog() flips the avatar to the left for Elora's replies.
- Placeholder avatar PNGs (a plain initialed circle each) stand in
  for real artwork.

application.mainClass now points at Launcher, so `./gradlew run` and
the shadowJar launch the GUI by default; `elora.Elora.main` still
exists for running the console version directly.

Manually verified: the window opens, shows the welcome bubble, and
round-trips a todo command correctly through Elora's existing logic.
`./gradlew build` still passes all 27 tests with zero Checkstyle
violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs to join Ui's multi-line messages
commitResults.messageBody:
Several Ui message methods built a fixed number of lines by hand
with "line1\n" + "line2\n" + "line3", repeating the same pattern
with slightly different literals each time.

Add a private joinLines(String...) helper and use it in
welcomeMessage(), taskAddedMessage(), taskMarkedMessage(),
taskUnmarkedMessage(), and taskDeletedMessage() - each call site now
just lists its lines instead of hand-splicing newlines between them.

taskListMessage(), matchingTasksMessage(), and tasksOnDateMessage()
are left as StringBuilder loops, since they iterate over a
runtime-sized list rather than a fixed number of lines - varargs
doesn't fit there without first collecting the loop into an array,
which would be more convoluted than the loop itself.

Verified the produced text is unchanged via a manual CLI run;
`./gradlew build` still passes all 27 tests with zero Checkstyle
violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add explicit JavaFX dependencies matching the SE-EDU tutorial
commitResults.messageBody:
The GUI compiled and ran fine locally because the Azul Zulu FX JDK
bundles JavaFX directly into the JDK image, so build.gradle declared
no JavaFX dependency at all. That's a portability trap: anyone
building this project on a plain (non-FX) JDK 25 - a different OS, a
CI runner, a grader's machine - would fail to even compile it, since
javafx.* wouldn't exist on their JDK's module path.

Add the exact dependency block from the SE-EDU JavaFX tutorial
(javafx-base/controls/fxml/graphics, each pinned to 17.0.7, for all
three win/mac/linux classifiers) rather than something invented for
this one machine. On this machine the bundled JDK's own JavaFX
classes still win via classloader parent delegation, so nothing
changes at runtime here; on a plain JDK these jars are what make the
app work at all.

Verified: `./gradlew clean build` passes (compile, all 27 tests,
zero Checkstyle violations), and the shadowJar still launches
correctly with these dependencies on the classpath.
